description: Declarative FRAME DATA classifying action/effect kinds as reversible (free exploration -- cheap, re-collapsible; the agent can re-run the fixpoint and try again) or committing (irreversible or externally-consequential -- expensive, must pass a gate before it happens). This generalizes a distinction the substrate already implements bespoke for ONE case: `run_rules` is a reversible monotone fixpoint (Tarski -- a rule can only ADD facts within a tick, so re-running it from the same state always reaches the same answer, nothing is lost by trying again), while `fold_clock_edge` (the DSL's 'tock', runners/dsl/src/py.rs ~line 2705) is the substrate's own lawful NON-MONOTONE down-stroke -- it is a SEPARATE phase from run_rules precisely because committing next_X -> X cannot be undone by re-running the fixpoint. domains/proposal_install.py's five-guardrail install gate is the same shape hand-built for ONE action class (runtime install: hot-swapping the agent's own .so). This seed makes the distinction a first-class, extensible PROPERTY OF THE ACTION/EFFECT KIND rather than a one-off, so any new action class gets the classification for free instead of a bespoke re-derivation.

microtheory.name: reversibility_frame
microtheory.description: commit-vs-explore (reversible vs committing) classification of action/effect kinds, read by domains/commitment_gate.py

default_reason: unclassified kind -- fail closed: an action/effect kind this frame has no entry for is treated as committing (gated) until a human/agent extends this file on purpose. Silence in the frame is never read as permission.

attrs.reason: In-graph mutation applied inside the run_rules fixpoint. run_rules is monotone (Tarski): a rule can only add facts within a tick, so the same starting state always reaches the same fixpoint regardless of how many times it is (re-)run. A node minted this way is re-collapsible -- if the surrounding reasoning turns out to be wrong, the agent re-collapses (re-derives) rather than needing to undo anything.
Same shape as add_node, plus dedup: reuses an existing witness instead of minting a duplicate. Still monotone, still in-fixpoint, still re-collapsible.
In-graph relation added inside the run_rules fixpoint. Same monotonicity argument as add_node -- adding a relation never removes a witness for a later re-derivation.

In-fixpoint attribute write. The rule-authoring convention (see fold_clock_edge's own doc comment) is that a rule reads CURRENT and writes NEXT_<attr> combinationally, never mutating its own inputs -- so set_attr during run_rules is exploratory scratch, not a commitment. (A rule that instead clobbers a CURRENT attr read by other rules in the same fixpoint is the one case this frame is deliberately conservative about -- see the discriminative note in domains/commitment_gate.py.)
Delta-only variant of set_attr -- a no-op when the value is unchanged, otherwise identical reasoning: in-fixpoint, re-collapsible.

Operates on a DISPOSABLE sandbox copy of the crate (self_extend_rust's cargo_check in a scratch dir, rust_runtime_world's validate_designs_in_sandbox) -- never the live tree. The whole point of the sandbox (see domains/rust_runtime_world.py's module docstring) is that anything that happens inside it is free to discard; nothing outside the sandbox root is ever touched, so there is nothing to revert.

Read-only query of graph state (node/nodes/neighbours/has_node, or ingesting a percept into the graph as new nodes covered by add_node above). Nothing is destroyed or sent outside the graph, so it is trivially reversible: reading twice never changes what is true.
Pure text templating (self_extend_rust.render_spec) -- builds fragment strings in memory, touches no file and no external resource. Calling it is exactly as free as calling it twice.

Destroys a node and its incident edges. Non-monotone: run_rules cannot re-derive exactly this deletion by re-running the fixpoint (Tarski monotonicity means a rule fixpoint can only prove MORE facts, never fewer) -- an explicit re-add afterwards is a NEW mutation, not an undo, and any downstream state that depended on the deleted node's identity (its NodeID) cannot be recovered even if content is re-added, because node ids recycle from a freelist (see CLAUDE.md's node-id caution).
Removes a relation. Same non-monotone-deletion argument as del_node: nothing in the monotone fixpoint can restore exactly this state on its own.

THE ARCHETYPE this whole frame generalizes from. runners/dsl/src/py.rs's fold_clock_edge is the substrate's own lawful non-monotone down-stroke: it commits next_<X> -> <X> on clocked nodes, in a SEPARATE phase from run_rules specifically because a value going DOWN is impossible inside the monotone in-tick fixpoint (Tarski) -- so the commit needs its OWN phase, after exploration is done, not interleaved with it (interleaving next-state computation and commit within one fixpoint IS the limit-cycle bug the doc comment there warns about). Every other 'committing' entry in this frame is a member of the same family: a down-stroke that must not be chased by further exploration until it is deliberately fired.

Hot-swaps the on-disk _native*.so via `maturin develop --release` (domains.self_extend.PrimitiveExtension.extend, called from domains/proposal_install.py). Changes the agent's own runtime for every future process that imports substrate_rs after the swap. This is the bespoke instance the whole frame generalizes: domains/proposal_install.py's five guardrails ARE a commit gate for exactly this one action class, built before this frame existed.

Reaches outside the graph to a live network resource (domains/fetch_dispatch.py's agent-authored http_get effector). The response is a fact about the outside world captured at read time -- the request itself may also have external side effects the agent cannot observe or undo (server-side state, rate limits, logs), and the exact same GET is not guaranteed repeatable (the resource can change or vanish).

Issues a real action (click/type/navigate) against a live BrowserWorld DOM session (worlds/browser.py, dispatched from domains/browse_dispatch.py). The target page's own state is external and not owned by the agent's graph -- a click can submit a form, follow a link, or trigger server-side effects that cannot be reversed by discarding the BrowserSession node.

Issues a real move against a live ARC game/world (domains/arc3_world.py, domains/arc3_thin.py apply_action). The world's own state machine advances whether or not the move was the right one -- there is no 'undo the last move' primitive in the world, only playing forward from wherever it lands.

Emits audible speech to the outside world (or any produced utterance handed to a world adapter for external playback). Once spoken, it cannot be unsaid -- unlike an in-graph Message node, which can simply not be selected for outbound emission.

domains/teach.py's SAVE half: appends the taught item to a seed manifest file (seeds/<category>.json) on disk. Persists across every future boot -- reverting requires a manual edit of the seed file outside the graph, not something the agent can undo from inside a tick. (The LIVE-graph half of teach() -- adding the node to the running substrate -- is itself an add_node and is reversible on its own; it is the disk write that makes teach() as a whole a commit.)

WorldAdapter.save overwriting an existing on-disk checkpoint that a future process resumes from. Overwriting the last good checkpoint with a bad one destroys the recovery point -- not undoable from inside the graph, only from a separate backup outside this system's control.
